newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Markets soar after British interest rate rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Markets soar after British interest rate rise.

text.p: British financial markets soared on Tuesday after new Labour finance minister Gordon Brown raised interest rates but, more importantly, gave the Bank of England freedom to set the cost of borrowing.
The quarter-point increase in official rates to 6.25 percent had been widely expected to prevent the economy overheating. But the radical overhaul of the central bank's responsibilities was not.

Brown said the Treasury would still set the inflation target -- which remains at 2.5 percent -- but the markets were delighted that interest rate decisions could not now be influenced by political considerations.
Government bonds soared more than two points while sterling hit a 4-1/2 year high, rising more than three pfennings to around 2.83 marks.
The stock market, already buoyed by the strength of Wall Street overnight, surged 70 points after Brown's statement, which followed a meeting this morning with Bank of England governor Eddie George.
The FTSE of 100 leading stocks was up 64 points at 4,519 at 1300 GMT, pushing further into record territory.

The markets' reaction indicated an early vote of confidence in the new Labour government, which won by a landslide in the May 1 election, after years in which dealers had regarded the old tax-and-spend Labour party with intense suspicion.
Analysts said the latest interest rate rise, even coupled with the Bank of England's new independence, did not signal the cost of borrowing would go much higher.
"Where rates go from here is not much higher," said John Shepperd, chief economist at securities house Yamaichi International.
Economist Richard Jeffrey of Charterhouse Tilney said the interest rate rise was not a surprise. "There was a clear need for rates to rise and Brown has decided to show his mettle," Jeffrey said.

Corey Miller of Credit Lyonnais Laing, also had praise for Brown, dubbed the "Iron Chancellor" during the election camapign after his pledge to stick to the then Conservative government's strict spending plans.
"By raising rates a quarter of a point it gets the pain out of the way early. It imposes some monetary constraints and gives him credibility. He's going down the right path," he said.
